items.title: Mimetic desire, social contagion, and the fight for your true self
items.description: In 1936, a shipyard worker in Hamburg kept his arms folded while hundreds of men around him raised theirs for Hitler. Luke Burgis, author of Wanting and The One in the 99, wants to know what it takes to become that person, and he traces the answer back to the family. items.title: 3 ways to find and nurture better friendships
items.description:
Why do you think anything is normal?

items.title: Why smart people stay stuck in research mode
items.description:
I recently had coffee with a university colleague who told me she was in the middle of planning a workshop. She had bought a couple of books about hosting workshops, had created a spreadsheet projecting attendance under different scenarios, and was now comparing ticketing platforms. But she still hadn’t invited a single person.

items.title: The 3 great origin mysteries: The universe, life, and consciousness
items.description:
Physicist and cosmologist Paul Davies, author of The Demon in the Machine, argues that the deepest mystery of life’s origin is how chemistry came to write its own code. 
 Davies traces the question from Aristotle and Schrödinger’s “aperiodic crystal” to Maxwell’s demon, Michael Levin’s two-headed flatworms, and the possibility of a shadow biosphere hiding on Earth. 
 This video  The 3 great origin mysteries: The universe, life, and consciousness  is featured on  Big Think .

items.title: Clinical psychologist: 5 types of narcissism and how to identify them
items.description:
Narcissistic people are often charming at the dinner party and cruel in the car ride home, which tells you they can control it. Clinical psychologist Ramani Durvasula, author of It’s Not You, has studied narcissism since long before it became a buzzword, and she argues that most of what circulates online gets it wrong. 
 This video  Clinical psychologist: 5 types of narcissism and how to identify them  is featured on  Big Think .

items.title: Stop trying to find yourself
items.description: Philosopher Joe Folley is skeptical that there’s a core self down there to find. In this Big Think Conversation with Jonny Thomson, he makes the case for a self that gets built rather than excavated — and argues that the attention it takes to build one has been quietly thinned down into something you spend, trade, and optimize. items.title: Free will: The real casualty of the algorithm
items.description:
In the deserts of fourth-century Egypt, monks described a strange affliction: a restless urge to be anywhere but where they were, attending to any reality but the one in front of them. They called it acedia. Luke Burgis, author of  Wanting: The Power of Mimetic Desire in Everyday Life , argues that our phones have made it socially contagious. 
 This video  Free will: The real casualty of the algorithm  is featured on  Big Think .

items.title: Ask Ethan: What should you do when a respected theory is false?
items.description: At every point in our quest to understand the world and universe — the one around us and the one within us — we can only start based on what we know and can imagine at present. We are biased by what we know and what we’re ignorant of, and we’re also influenced by the range of experiences that we’re aware of.
